newsitem.title: JAPAN: No signs yet of Japan quakes ceasing, agency says.
newsitem.headline: No signs yet of Japan quakes ceasing, agency says.

text.p: The near-constant rumbling of minor earthquakes unnerving a seaside resort near Tokyo for 48 hours shows no sign of ceasing, the Meteorological Agency said on Tuesday.

"The tremors are only at a beginning stage and we still see no signs of the earthquake swarm ending," Akio Yoshida of the Earthquake Prediction Information Division at the Meteorological Agency told a news conference.

Since Monday, more than 2,600 minor tremors, including two which may indicate volcanic activity, hit the city of Ito, on the coast of the Izu Peninsula 120 km (75 miles) southwest of Tokyo. Of the total, 86 were strong enough to be felt, the agency said.
Three people were slightly injured by falling objects but there had been no reports of major damage, police said.
The strongest tremor so far measured 5.7 on the Richter scale and came at 12.51 p.m. (0351 GMT) on Tuesday. It was felt as far away as Tokyo.
A quake of that size is capable of causing damage in populated areas.
The agency said the shallowness of the epicentres and two "low-frequency" quakes pointed to undersea volcanic activity.
"Volcanic activity is not always the cause of these low-frequency tremors, but they did occur just before a undersea volcano erupted in 1989," an agency seismologist said.
A small underwater eruption off Ito in 1989 caused a tremor measuring 5.5 on the Richter scale but no damage.
"Low-frequency tremors often accompany earthquake swarms, but earthquake swarms in this area have never led to a major earthquake in the past," said Katsuyuki Abe, a seismologist at Tokyo University.
"The 1989 tremors were closer to land than the current tremors, so the damage this time would probably be limited," Abe said.
The agency said it had sent seismologists and vulcanologists to the region to step up monitoring activity.
One of the stronger tremors late on Monday triggered a small landslide which destroyed a warehouse. Ito police officials reported over 20 incidents in the city where water and gas mains were severed.
"We hope tourists won't may start avoiding Izu again," said Tadashi Makino of Ito City Tourist Association. Ito, a city of 72,000 people, is a popular resort famous for hot springs and seafood.
Last October, Ito was shaken by an earthquake swarm of more than 5,000 tremors, only a few of which could be felt. There was no damage.
